prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Come live with me, and be my love, And we will some new pleasures prove Of golden sands, and crystal brooks, With silken lines, and silver hooks. There will the river whispering run Warm'd by thy eyes, more than the sun; And there the 'enamour'd fish will stay, Begging themselves they may betray. When thou wilt swim in that live bath, Each fish, which every channel hath, Will amorously to thee swim, Gladder to catch thee, than thou him. If thou, to be so seen, be'st loth, By sun or moon, thou dark'nest both, And if myself have leave to see, I need not their light having thee. Let others freeze with angling reeds, And cut their legs with shells and weeds, Or treacherously poor fish beset, With strangling snare, or windowy net. Let coarse bold hands from slimy nest The bedded fish in banks out-wrest; Or curious traitors, sleeve-silk flies, Bewitch poor fishes' wand'ring eyes. For thee, thou need'st no such deceit, For thou thyself art thine own bait: That fish, that is not catch'd thereby, Alas, is wiser far than I.

Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Come, And, With

outputs.L1:
Come live with me, and be my love,  
And we shall prove new pleasures there:  
Golden sands and crystal brooks,  
Silken lines and silver hooks.

There the river, whispering, will run,  
Warmed by your eyes more than by the sun;  
And there the enamoured fish will stay,  
Begging that they may themselves betray.

When you swim in that living bath,  
Each fish in every channel there  
Will lovingly swim toward you,  
Happier to catch you than you are to catch it.

If you are reluctant to be seen  
By sun or moon, you darken both;  
And if I am granted leave to look upon you,  
I need no light from them, having you.

Let others freeze with angling reeds,  
And cut their legs on shells and weeds;  
Let them treacherously beset poor fish  
With strangling snares or windowed nets.

Let coarse, bold hands from slimy nests  
Wrest the bedded fish from the banks;  
Or let curious traitors, with sleeve-silk flies,  
Bewitch the wandering eyes of poor fishes.

For you need no such deceit:  
You yourself are your own bait.  
The fish that is not caught thereby—  
Alas—is far wiser than I.
outputs.L2:
Come and dwell beside me, and be the one I love; together we shall discover fresh delights among shining sands and clear-running streams, using silken cords and hooks of silver. There the river will glide with a murmuring sound, warmed more by your eyes than by the sun itself; and the lovestruck fish will linger there, almost pleading to give themselves away.

When you choose to bathe in that living water, every fish in every current will swim toward you with desire, happier to be captured by you than you would be to catch it. If you are unwilling to be looked upon by either sun or moon, your presence will outshine and dim them both; and if I am allowed to gaze at you, I will have no need of their light.

Let others shiver while fishing with rods, and let them wound their legs on shells and weeds. Let them cruelly trap helpless fish with choking snares or transparent nets. Let rough, clumsy hands drag fish from their muddy beds along the banks, or let cunning deceivers use silk-made flies to enchant the wandering eyes of poor fish.

But for you, no trickery is necessary. You are yourself the lure. Any fish not caught by such a charm, alas, is far wiser than I am.
outputs.L3:
The speaker invites his beloved to come and live with him, promising that together they will discover new pleasures in a beautiful and peaceful natural world. He imagines an idyllic landscape filled with golden sands, clear streams, and crystal brooks, a place where love and nature exist in perfect harmony. This setting is not merely a background for romance; it becomes part of the speaker’s vision of happiness, offering both beauty and delight to the beloved if she accepts his invitation.

Throughout the poem, nature itself seems enchanted by the beloved’s beauty. The rivers, sunlight, moonlight, and even the fish appear to respond to her presence. Her beauty is presented as a force powerful enough to transform the natural world, making it brighter, livelier, and more magical. The speaker suggests that wherever she goes, the world around her becomes more radiant and responsive, as though nature recognizes and celebrates her charm.

The beloved is also described as so brilliant and luminous that the speaker needs no other source of light if he is allowed to look upon her. Her beauty outshines ordinary sunlight and moonlight, becoming a kind of guiding illumination for him. This exaggeration emphasizes the depth of his admiration and devotion. To the speaker, her presence is enough to brighten the world and fulfill his desires.

The poem also contrasts ordinary methods of fishing with the beloved’s natural power of attraction. Typical fishing depends on deception, using bait, hooks, and tricks to capture fish. The beloved, however, does not need such artificial methods. Her beauty alone is enough to draw the fish toward her. This comparison elevates her charm above human craft and cunning, suggesting that her power is effortless, honest, and irresistible.

In the conclusion, the speaker reflects that any fish able to resist the beloved’s beauty must be wiser than he is. Unlike such a fish, he has been completely captured by her charm. This final thought blends humor with sincere admiration: the speaker recognizes his own helplessness in love, admitting that he is willingly and entirely captivated by the beloved’s radiant beauty.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a seductive invitation in which the speaker urges his beloved to join him in a peaceful natural setting of rivers, brooks, and clear streams. Like a traditional pastoral love poem, it imagines the countryside as an ideal place of pleasure, beauty, and intimacy. The speaker describes an inviting world where the lovers can sit together beside the water and enjoy the gentle movement of fish, the brightness of the stream, and the sweetness of the surrounding landscape.

At the same time, the poem uses fishing as an extended metaphor for love and desire. The speaker imagines his beloved as someone whose beauty has the power to attract all living things around her. Fish are drawn to her not because of hooks, nets, or artificial bait, but because she herself is irresistibly appealing. Her presence transforms the act of fishing into an image of attraction and surrender. The fish willingly approach her, just as the speaker himself is captivated by her charm.

By the end of the poem, the speaker suggests that his beloved does not need any artificial lure at all. Her beauty alone is powerful enough to serve as bait. This conclusion emphasizes her extraordinary attractiveness and the control she has over others. She can capture fish without effort, and, more importantly, she has already captured the speaker’s heart. In this way, the poem blends pastoral imagery, playful wit, and erotic suggestion to celebrate the beloved’s irresistible power.
outputs.L5:
**Come and With**

“Come” is an invitation. It asks someone to move closer, to join, to begin.  
“And” is a connection. It brings ideas, people, and moments together.  
“With” is a promise of company. It means not being alone.

Together, these simple words create a feeling of welcome: **Come and be with us.** They remind us that life is better when shared—with friends, with family, with hope, and with kindness. A small invitation can open the door to new experiences, and a simple connection can turn an ordinary moment into something meaningful.

counterfactuals.prompt: Recite John Donne’s poem “The Bait” in full.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Bait**  
*by John Donne*

Come live with me, and be my love,  
And we will some new pleasures prove  
Of golden sands, and crystal brooks,  
With silken lines, and silver hooks.  

There will the river whispering run  
Warmed by thy eyes, more than the sun;  
And there the enamoured fish will stay,  
Begging themselves they may betray.  

When thou wilt swim in that live bath,  
Each fish, which every channel hath,  
Will amorously to thee swim,  
Gladder to catch thee, than thou him.  

If thou, to be so seen, be’st loth,  
By sun or moon, thou darkenest both;  
And if myself have leave to see,  
I need not their light, having thee.  

Let others freeze with angling reeds,  
And cut their legs with shells and weeds,  
Or treacherously poor fish beset,  
With strangling snare, or windowy net.  

Let coarse bold hands from slimy nest  
The bedded fish in banks out-wrest;  
Or curious traitors, sleeve-silk flies,  
Bewitch poor fishes’ wandering eyes.  

For thee, thou need’st no such deceit,  
For thou thyself art thine own bait:  
That fish, that is not catched thereby,  
Alas, is wiser far than I.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1
